title: Regional commissioning: budget impact of extended pharmacy hours, meta-analysis withdrawn for a two-strand mixed-methods review
notes: Expert path. A commissioning economist asks for a systematic review of extended community pharmacy opening in two parts that must not be merged (routing explicit systematic-review; the need avoids naming any other design). A fixture search returns eight budget and practice records; the appraisal records six claims. The first design decision (a meta-analysis of budget impact, resting on c1 and c2) is accepted with its one gate met; the analysis stage then shows that pooling two or three incompatible budget estimates is not defensible, the investigator withdraws the accepted decision (kept as withdrawn), and a revised design reply proposes a convergent segregated mixed-methods systematic review resting on c1, c3, c4 and c5 with one gate met and a data governance gate unknown (accepted selection, blocked action). The design change after Protocol and Analysis were completed flags both for review (G8), and both are redone: the revised protocol has one primary outcome per strand (budget impact for the payer, and synthesised practice findings, patient-centred) with a process and a balancing outcome, and an outcome with the invalid role 'cost-driver' that must be dropped with invalid-enum and dropped issues rather than demoted. Record ids are stableRecordId values as in src/lib/evidence/records.ts at 875fe59: DOI hash for records 1, 3, 4, 5, 7 (ev-1cvugeb, ev-09c44mm, ev-1l5ehvn, ev-1jy7fry, ev-0uuyulh); titleYearKey hash for records 2, 6, 8 (ev-1hod7pl, ev-0wssqfd, ev-1kh3m6o). Requires S11 (selectionStatus, actionStatus, withdrawal, basis), S13 (appraisal) and D5 (status text, review required). Catches: a pooled figure forced from incompatible estimates, an accepted decision erased instead of withdrawn, downstream stages left current after the design changes, two strand-specific primary outcomes collapsed into one, and an invalid outcome role silently relabelled.

inputs.need:
I am a health economist in the commissioning team of a regional health authority covering about 1.3 million people. Our board has to decide by March 2027 whether to fund extended opening hours for community pharmacies: 40 pharmacies would open until 22:00 on weekdays and from 10:00 to 18:00 on Sundays, for a supplement of about 2.1 million a year. The case for it is that pharmacists would handle minor ailments and emergency supply of medicines out of hours, taking pressure off the out-of-hours GP service and the emergency departments. The case against is that most of the evidence comes from pharmacy bodies and that late-night staffing may be unsafe or impossible to sustain.

Before we commission any local modelling I want a systematic review of what is already known, in two parts that should not be squashed into one number. First, the evidence on what extended hours cost and what they save from the payer's point of view: out-of-hours GP contacts and emergency department visits avoided, medicines supplied, and the resulting budget impact over three years. Second, what pharmacists, commissioners, other clinicians and members of the public have said about how extended hours work in practice: who uses late opening, whether it reaches shift workers and people without a regular GP, staffing and lone working at night, and whether demand simply moves from one service to another.

I have one analyst for six months, access to the main bibliographic sources through our library service, and our own out-of-hours activity data if we need local prices later. I would like help defining the review questions and eligibility criteria, choosing the outcomes for each part and saying which is primary, deciding how to combine or not combine budget figures from different health systems and years, appraising the studies of people's views, and bringing the two parts together for the board. If the evidence cannot support a pooled estimate, I would rather say so than force one.
inputs.constraints: One analyst from October 2026 to March 2027; library access to bibliographic sources; no primary data collection; board decision in March 2027; any local re-pricing must use the authority's out-of-hours activity data, which needs the data governance lead's approval.

response.title: Extended community pharmacy opening hours: budget impact and how the service works in practice
response.subtitle: Systematic review in two strands for a commissioning decision
response.statement: A regional health authority must decide by March 2027 whether to pay about 2.1 million a year for 40 community pharmacies to open late on weekdays and on Sundays. The claimed savings from avoided out-of-hours GP contacts and emergency department visits are uncertain and mostly estimated by pharmacy bodies, and the practicalities of late-night staffing are contested. A systematic review is needed that keeps the budget impact evidence and the evidence on how the service works in practice separate, then brings them together for the board.
response.whoAffected: Residents who need medicines or advice out of hours, especially shift workers and people without a registered GP; community pharmacists and owners; out-of-hours GP and emergency department services; the commissioning board and its budget.
response.whatHurts: Paying for a service that does not reduce demand elsewhere would divert money from other care; refusing a service that reaches people with nowhere else to go could push them to emergency departments; unsafe lone working could harm pharmacy staff.
response.currentPractice: A few pharmacies open late on their own account; out-of-hours minor ailments and emergency supply go to the out-of-hours GP service or emergency departments; previous commissioning papers relied on advocacy estimates.
response.whyNow: A board decision in March 2027 and one funded analyst from October 2026 to March 2027.
response.constraints: One analyst for six months; no primary data collection; local re-pricing needs the data governance lead's approval, not yet requested; the two strands must not be merged into one number.
response.patientCenteredGoal: People who need medicines or advice in the evening or on Sunday can get them safely and close to home, and the authority spends its budget where it reduces unmet need.
response.summary: Problem framed as a systematic review with a budget impact strand and a practice-and-views strand for a funding decision.

records.title: Extended opening hours in community pharmacies and out-of-hours general practice contacts: a regional before-after evaluation with a comparison region
records.authors: Brathwaite-Okoro L, Nilsson-Achebe D, Farouk-Hemming S
records.abstract: In one region, 34 community pharmacies extended their opening to 22:00 on weekdays and opened on Sundays for 18 months; a neighbouring region served as comparison. Out-of-hours GP contacts for minor ailments fell by 6 percent relative to the comparison region, and emergency supplies of medicines through the out-of-hours GP service fell by 11 percent. From the payer's perspective, the extended-hours supplement cost 1.8 million a year and valued offsets were 1.4 million, a net annual budget impact of an extra 0.4 million. Emergency department attendances for minor conditions did not change clearly. Pharmacy staffing costs above the supplement were not included.

records.title: Budget impact of late-night community pharmacy opening: a decision model for an urban health board
records.abstract: We built a three-year budget impact model of late-night opening for 25 pharmacies serving 600,000 people, from the health board's perspective. Inputs came from pharmacy consultation logs, published unit costs and expert opinion. The base case gave a net cost of 1.2 million over three years. Results were most sensitive to the share of late-night pharmacy consultations that would otherwise have led to an emergency department attendance, which experts placed between 5 and 25 percent; at 25 percent the scheme saved money. The authors call for empirical data on what users would have done without the pharmacy.

records.title: Sunday opening of community pharmacies and emergency department attendances for minor conditions: an interrupted time series
records.abstract: We analysed weekly emergency department attendances for minor conditions in four towns for two years before and one year after local pharmacies began opening on Sundays. There was no clear change in level or trend of Sunday attendances for minor conditions (level change minus 2 percent, 95 percent CI minus 9 to 6). Attendances for minor conditions on Monday mornings also did not change. The analysis did not include costs. The authors note that Sunday opening was advertised only in pharmacies and that awareness among residents was probably low during the first year.

records.title: Who uses community pharmacies after 20:00? Late-evening consultations in two cities
records.abstract: Pharmacists in 18 late-opening pharmacies in two cities logged 1,850 consultations between 20:00 and closing over four weeks. Emergency supply of a regular medicine made up 38 percent of consultations and minor ailments 27 percent. Users were younger than daytime users and more often shift workers, and 22 percent of users had no registered GP. Pharmacists judged that 31 percent of users would otherwise have contacted the out-of-hours GP service and 9 percent an emergency department, but users were not asked directly. Consultations peaked between 20:00 and 21:00 and were few after 21:30.

records.title: Pharmacists' experience of working extended hours: staffing, lone working and safety
records.abstract: We conducted in-depth conversations with 24 pharmacists and 9 pharmacy owners in regions that had funded extended opening. Pharmacists described lone working late at night, fear of aggression and theft, and fatigue after long shifts. Owners reported difficulty recruiting pharmacists for evenings and relied on locums, which raised costs above the supplement. Four of the nine owners had reduced their hours within a year. Pharmacists valued being able to help people who had nowhere else to go, but several said the late hours were quiet after 21:00. Participants suggested shared rotas between neighbouring pharmacies and security measures as conditions for continuing.

records.title: Commissioners' views on paying for extended pharmacy access: a thematic analysis of board papers and discussions
records.abstract: We analysed board papers from eleven health authorities that considered extended pharmacy opening between 2014 and 2019 and held discussions with 16 commissioners. Commissioners valued convenience and visible access but doubted claims of savings, because avoided contacts were estimated by pharmacists rather than observed. Several worried that demand moved from daytime services rather than falling. Decisions were often made on the strength of advocacy from pharmacy bodies. Commissioners asked for evidence separated by who uses late opening and for costs that included staffing above the supplement.

records.title: Combining budget impact estimates from different payers: a methodological review of 42 syntheses
records.authors: Gallardo-Whitmore E, Tanaka-Osei B, Lindberg-Ruiz H
records.abstract: We reviewed 42 evidence syntheses that combined budget impact analyses. Studies differed in perspective, price year, currency, time horizon and the services counted as offsets, and fewer than half reported all five. Pooling budget impact figures across health systems produced estimates that could not be interpreted for any single payer. We recommend structured tables that re-express each estimate in a common price year and currency, report perspective and offsets explicitly, and avoid a pooled figure unless the studies share perspective and setting. Where local decisions are needed, estimates should be re-priced with local unit costs.

records.title: Public views of late-night pharmacy services: a citizens' panel report
records.abstract: A panel of 48 residents discussed late-night pharmacy services over two sessions. Participants valued being able to get medicines and advice after work, especially people working shifts and parents of young children. People without a car said a late pharmacy was only useful if it was on a bus route that ran after 21:00. Some worried about waiting alone late at night and about privacy at the counter. Participants were unsure whether they would have gone to the emergency department instead. The panel recommended publicising late opening and placing late pharmacies near public transport and health centres.

response.synthesis: Eight retrieved records, appraised at abstract level. Only one empirical costing exists: offsets covered most but not all of the supplement (net extra 0.4 million a year) and excluded staffing costs above the supplement. A decision model turns on the unknown share of users who would otherwise attend an emergency department, and a time series found no clear change in such attendances after Sunday opening. Late users are younger, often shift workers, and a fifth have no registered GP. Pharmacists and owners describe lone working, fatigue and costly locums, and some schemes shrank within a year. Commissioners doubt pharmacist-estimated savings. A methods review advises against pooling budget figures across health systems.
response.gradeRationale: Budget evidence rests on one before-after costing and one model with expert inputs; practice evidence is qualitative and consistent. Certainty that extended hours save money is very low; certainty about who uses them and what staffing involves is low to moderate. Overall low.
response.summary: Eight retrieved records appraised; six source-derived claims recorded; overall certainty low.

steps.note: Appraisal of eight retrieved records (S13). Claim c6 is marked high uncertainty because the time series ran while awareness was low.

response.reading: The budget question and the practice question meet at the counterfactual: what late-night users would have done without the pharmacy. Budget figures depend on it and it is estimated, not observed. Staffing costs and lone working determine whether the service lasts. Access for shift workers and people without a registered GP is the main equity case, and demand moving from daytime services is the main threat to savings.

response.designSummary: Systematic review with random-effects meta-analysis of net annual budget impact per 100,000 population, as specified in the accepted design.
response.sampleSize: A review has no sample size in the trial sense; the question is whether enough comparable estimates exist. The retrieved records contain two budget impact estimates (a before-after costing and a decision model) and one time series without costs, from different health systems, price years and perspectives, and a methods review advises against pooling such figures (c3). With two or three heterogeneous estimates, the between-study variance cannot be estimated and a pooled figure would be driven by the model's expert assumption about emergency attendances (c2). The meta-analysis in the accepted design is therefore not defensible; a structured synthesis in common prices, with budget impact shown across counterfactual assumptions, is the honest alternative.
response.primaryAnalysis: As specified: DerSimonian-Laird random-effects pooling of net annual budget impact. Not recommended for the reasons above; the design decision should be revisited before the protocol is registered.
response.secondaryAnalysis: Narrative summary of views; no formal synthesis method specified in the accepted design.
response.missingData: Studies not reporting perspective or price year would be excluded from pooling, which would leave at most one estimate.
response.multiplicity: Not applicable to a single pooled estimate.
overfittingGuards: Do not pool fewer than three comparable estimates

The strands are integrated in a joint display that maps who uses late opening and what it costs to staff against the budget figures.

response.procedures: Search of four bibliographic sources, commissioning papers and pharmacy body reports from 2005; dual screening of 20 percent; separate extraction forms for each strand; budget figures re-priced to 2026 with the authority's out-of-hours unit costs once data governance approves; thematic synthesis of practice findings; joint display built after both strands are complete.

outcomes.name: Net budget impact for the payer (budget strand)
outcomes.measure: Scheme cost minus valued offsets per year, re-expressed in 2026 prices and shown across counterfactual assumptions for each study
outcomes.timing: Per year, up to three years
outcomes.why: The board's budget question, without a pooled figure (claim c3).

outcomes.name: How extended hours work in practice (practice strand)
outcomes.measure: Synthesised findings on access, staffing, safety and displacement, each with a GRADE-CERQual confidence rating
outcomes.why: The board's second question; a different kind of evidence with its own primary outcome.

outcomes.name: Avoided contacts per 1,000 late consultations
outcomes.measure: Out-of-hours GP contacts and emergency attendances avoided, as reported or estimated

outcomes.name: Reporting completeness of budget studies
outcomes.measure: Share of budget studies reporting perspective, price year, currency, horizon and offsets
outcomes.why: Shows how far each estimate can be trusted.

outcomes.name: Displacement of demand
outcomes.measure: Evidence that daytime pharmacy or GP use fell as late use rose
outcomes.why: Savings are illusory if demand only moves.

outcomes.name: Staffing premium for late shifts
outcomes.measure: Locum and security costs above the supplement

response.designSummary: Structured synthesis of budget figures in common prices and thematic synthesis of practice findings, integrated in a joint display; no meta-analysis.
response.sampleSize: No sample size applies. Based on the retrieved records and the search yield of similar reviews, the budget strand is expected to include three to six studies and the practice strand eight to fifteen. With so few budget studies, precision comes from showing each estimate across counterfactual assumptions, not from pooling.
response.primaryAnalysis: Budget strand: each estimate re-expressed in 2026 prices and the authority's perspective, tabulated with perspective, horizon, offsets and funding source, and recalculated at counterfactual emergency attendance shares of 5, 15 and 25 percent. Practice strand: line-by-line coding, descriptive then analytical themes, with GRADE-CERQual confidence for each finding.
response.secondaryAnalysis: Joint display mapping practice findings (who uses late opening, staffing, displacement) against budget components; discordance is reported. Certainty of budget findings is rated with GRADE adapted for economic evidence.
response.missingData: Missing perspective or price year is recorded and the estimate is re-priced only where assumptions can be stated; authors are contacted once.
response.software: Spreadsheet re-pricing template checked by a second analyst; qualitative coding in NVivo.
overfittingGuards: Counterfactual shares fixed in the protocol
response.summary: No meta-analysis; re-priced structured tables across counterfactual assumptions, thematic synthesis with CERQual, and a joint display.

response.risks: No participants are recruited; the risks are misleading the board with a single figure and overstating advocacy-funded evidence.
response.consent: Not applicable to a review of published and grey literature; re-pricing uses aggregated activity data without individual records.
response.data: Only aggregated out-of-hours activity counts and unit costs are used, after the data governance lead's approval; no individual-level data leave the authority's systems.
response.equity: PROGRESS-Plus: shift workers, people without a registered GP, people without a car and parents of young children are the main potential beneficiaries, and pharmacy location near late public transport decides who is reached. Both strands extract these characteristics, and the joint display shows who benefits alongside the cost.
response.effectiveness: The review informs whether the supplement buys access for people poorly served elsewhere, not only whether it saves money.
response.efficiency: One analyst and existing library access; no new data collection.
response.costs: Analyst time within existing funding; about two weeks of re-pricing work after approval.
response.partnerships: Local pharmaceutical committee (grey literature and context), out-of-hours GP provider, two members of the public from the citizens' health panel reviewing the plain-language summary, and the data governance lead.
response.rebPath: A review of published literature does not need research ethics review; the use of aggregated activity data for re-pricing needs the data governance lead's approval, which has not been requested, so that gate is unknown.
response.limitations: Few budget studies from comparable systems; counterfactual assumptions dominate; much of the evidence is funded by advocates.
response.summary: No participants; equity analysis of who benefits; the data governance gate for re-pricing is unknown.

response.partnershipPlan: Two members of the citizens' health panel review the review questions and the plain-language summary; the local pharmaceutical committee and the out-of-hours GP provider comment on the joint display before it goes to the board.
response.socialListening: No social media listening; public comments submitted to the authority's consultation on pharmacy services in the last two years are read for mentions of late opening.

items.quote: Composite paraphrase: I finish at nine; if the pharmacy shuts at six I either wait until my day off or go to the hospital.

items.implication: Show budget figures across counterfactual assumptions.

items.implication: Keep displacement as a balancing outcome.

response.title: Budget impact and practice of extended community pharmacy opening: a convergent segregated mixed-methods systematic review
response.abstract: Objective: to synthesise evidence on the budget impact of extending community pharmacy opening into evenings and Sundays, and on how extended hours work in practice. Design: convergent segregated mixed-methods systematic review with a budget strand re-priced to 2026 and a practice-and-views strand synthesised thematically, integrated in a joint display. Primary outcomes: net budget impact for the payer shown across counterfactual assumptions; synthesised findings on access, staffing, safety and displacement. Results and conclusions will be written after the review.
response.introduction: Health authorities are asked to fund extended pharmacy opening on the strength of claimed savings. Existing costings depend on what users would otherwise have done, and the practicalities of late-night staffing are rarely costed.
response.methods: Searches of four bibliographic sources and grey literature from 2005; separate eligibility, extraction and appraisal for each strand; no meta-analysis because budget figures differ in perspective, price year and offsets. Confidence in practice findings is rated with GRADE-CERQual.
response.results: No data have been extracted yet. The report will present the flow of studies for each strand, the re-priced budget table, the thematic findings with confidence ratings, and the joint display.
response.discussion: The discussion will set the budget figures beside who uses late opening and what it costs to staff, and state what the evidence can and cannot tell the board.
response.limitations: Few comparable budget studies; counterfactual assumptions dominate; advocacy funding; grey literature of variable quality.
response.conclusion: To be written after the review; it will not report a pooled budget figure.
response.reportingChecklist: PRISMA 2020 with JBI mixed-methods guidance and CHEERS 2022 items for extracted economic data
response.summary: PRISMA-structured draft with two strands; results empty until extraction.

manuscript.conclusion.includes: will not report a pooled budget figure
